(EC 2024) introduced a semi-random model for non-additive fair division in which each agent starts with an arbitrary base valuation over bundles of items and independently permutes the item names uniformly at random. While they proved that envy-free allocations exist with high probability as the number of items grows for $n = 2$ agents, they left open whether the same holds for $n > 2$ agents. We resolve this open question in the affirmative: for any fixed number of agents $n$ and any number of items $m$ divisible by $n$, an envy-free allocation exists with probability $1 - o(1)$ as $m \to \infty$. Our proof combines the second moment method with a connection to the (small-set) expansion of generalized Johnson graphs, which may be of independent interest.

title: Stable matching under regulation
abstract: In a market in which any coalition can reach agreements, a stable outcome need not exist even when agents have substitutable preferences. We show how regulation can restore stability. If a regulator participates in every agreement, a setwise stable outcome exists when each ordinary agent's preference satisfies a condition weaker than substitutability, while the regulator's preference remains largely unrestricted. An alternative existence result allows ordinary agents to have arbitrary preferences while requiring the regulator to support each agent's profitable contract deletions. Our results apply to matching markets involving regulated activities.

title: Pricing Information in Search with Nonobligatory Inspection
abstract: As AI agents reshape Web search and advertising, platforms can monetize information that improves decisions. We study information pricing for sequential search among independent alternatives with nonobligatory inspection: the buyer may select any alternative without buying its report. We show that a common fee maximizes static revenue for identical priors, resolving a uniform-pricing conjecture. Our results also establish that exact optimization is NP-hard for heterogeneous binary priors. Despite this hardness, our polynomial-time static pricing algorithm achieves a $3$-approximation to the information surplus. More generally, a common static fee approximates optimal adaptive revenue within a logarithmic factor in the number of alternatives. This guarantee is asymptotically tight.

title: QuantileMix: A Python package for quantile g-computation
abstract: Health researchers often study how a mixture of pollutants or nutrients relates to health. Quantile g-computation addresses this question by giving each exposure an ordered score and fitting a model for the outcome. For example, dividing an exposure into four quantile groups gives scores 0, 1, 2, and 3. The model can compare score 1 with score 2 for every exposure at once. These groups need not contain equal numbers of observations when measurements are tied. A one-score increase can represent different changes in the original units for different exposures. QuantileMix provides selected quantile g-computation methods in Python. It returns estimates, confidence intervals, predictions, and diagnostics for continuous, binary, count, and survival outcomes. Other models handle measurement limits, outcomes with several categories, and counts with many zeros. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy and do not require R. The package includes a reference manual, runnable examples, and numerical comparisons with R.

title: Inference for Causal Path-Specific Effects in Longitudinal Studies with Repeated Treatments and Multiple Mediators
abstract: In longitudinal studies, repeated treatments may be followed by different sequences of mediators and time-varying covariates. We develop semiparametric inference for path-specific effects in this setting, allowing the number, type, and ordering of intermediate variables to vary across treatment occasions. Under consistency, positivity, edge consistency, and the cross-world restrictions of a nonparametric structural equation model with independent errors, path-specific means are identified by the edge g-formula. We derive two parameterizations of the efficient influence function of the identifying functional. The first follows the observed-data factorization and uses conditional intermediate-variable densities. The second uses sequential regressions to replace the corresponding integrations and Bayes' rule to express density ratios through treatment-history regressions, thereby avoiding direct estimation of intermediate-variable densities. Each yields a one-step estimator that permits flexible nuisance estimation. We establish product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and semiparametric efficiency. The density-based estimator has blockwise multiple robustness, generalizing triply robust estimation, while the regression-based estimator has sequential multiple robustness. We further develop a sensitivity analysis for selected violations of cross-world independence assumptions used to identify these effects. Simulations examine finite-sample performance and robustness to model misspecifications. An application to the Framingham Heart Study examines sustained-smoking effects on systolic blood pressure along pathways through repeated body mass index measurements. The proposed methods are implemented in the R package flexPaths on Gihub at xxou/flexPaths.

title: Complete Cancer Prevalence Predictions via LASSO Regularization and Flexible Parametric Survival Cure Models
abstract: Cancer prevalence is a key measure of disease burden, and accurate projections are essential for healthcare planning and resource allocation. The Prevalence Incidence Analysis Model (PIAMOD) is widely used to estimate and project cancer prevalence in population-based studies by combining incidence rates and net survival within a forward calculation framework. We propose an improved approach to projecting cancer prevalence by using regularization techniques to select the optimal incidence model and flexible parametric survival cure models to improve the estimation of net survival. The proposed and conventional approaches were compared through a simulation study and an application to population-based data on patients diagnosed with colon cancer in Sweden between 1958 and 2019. Applying the proposed methodology, colon cancer prevalence in Sweden was projected through 2030. The number of individuals living with a previous diagnosis of colon cancer is projected to continue increasing, reaching approximately 550 per 100\,000 males and 500 per 100\,000 females by 2030. Careful model selection is essential when estimating measures of disease burden such as cancer prevalence. The projected increase in colon cancer prevalence in Sweden reflects continued improvements in survival for both sexes and highlights the growing number of individuals living with colon cancer.

title: Nonlinear Reduced-Bias Extreme Value Index Estimators: A Comparative Study
authors: Frederico Caeiro and M. Ivette Gomes
abstract: The estimation of the extreme value index (EVI) plays a central role in extreme value theory (EVT), particularly in the statistical modelling of heavy-tailed phenomena. Classical semi-parametric estimators of the EVI are known to suffer from substantial bias, especially for moderate sample sizes and for common choices of the number of upper order statistics. In recent years, several reduced-bias (RB) methodologies have been proposed in order to improve finite-sample performance while preserving asymptotic efficiency. In this paper, we present new classes of nonlinear RB EVI-estimators based on power mean-type and Lehmer mean-type functionals of upper log-excesses. Under a unified higher-order framework, asymptotic representations are derived and bias and variance properties are compared relative to other RB EVI classes introduced in the literature. An asymptotic comparison at optimal levels is conducted to identify regions of the space parameter where the proposed estimators are more efficient. A comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation study assesses the finite sample behaviour of the new estimators for several heavy tailed models. The results show that nonlinear reduced-bias estimators can provide improvements in bias and root mean squared error, although their relative performance depends on the underlying distribution and the choice of the tuning parameter. An application to hydrological data illustrates their practical use and the importance of threshold selection in EVI estimation.

title: Weighted Fairness in Multi-User Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling
abstract: As constellations of satellite grow in size, and become more costly, they are increasingly funded by multiple stakeholders who expect access to the constellation's resources that is commensurate with their investment. Such cooperation raises significant challenges for constellation operation, in particular regarding the fairness of the computed schedules among stakeholders. While several existing works deal with fairness in the Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling Problem (EOSSP), most of them assume that users (e.g. space agencies, research labs, countries) have the same weights, i.e. contributed equally to the project and therefore have equal access to the constellation. However, in practice, users' contributions often differ significantly. Hence, in this paper, we study a weighted variant of the EOSSP where users are assigned weights reflecting their respective contributions to the constellation. We propose several solution concepts with varying focus on efficiency and fairness, namely weighted utilitarianism, weighted egalitarianism, weighted leximin, and weighted ordered weighed averaging (WOWA). We formulate the related optimization problems as Mixed-Integer Linear Programs (MILPs), and compare them against two natural heuristics: weighted greedy and weighted round robin. All methods are evaluated on scenarios drawn from the literature, under strict runtime constraints, in order to assess the performance of each approach with respect to both efficiency and fairness metrics.

title: A Truthful-in-Expectation 2-Approximation for Pair-Specific Cascade Auctions in AI-Generated Content
abstract: Generative AI interfaces can insert sponsored content at multiple points in an answer, where click-through rates (CTRs) depend on the advertiser-position pair. Under the cascade model, users read ads sequentially and stop after their first click, so both ad assignment and display order affect welfare. For arbitrary pair-specific CTRs, Balseiro et al. (WWW 2026) gave a $4/(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation whose monotonicity has not been established, and a monotone $O(\log m)$-approximation for $m$ candidate positions. Earlier truthful constant-factor mechanisms require factorized CTR models and do not apply. Whether monotonicity is compatible with a constant-factor approximation in this general setting was left open by that work. We give a polynomial-time mechanism for arbitrary pair-specific CTRs and any limit on displayed ads that is truthful and individually rational in expectation and achieves a 2-approximation to optimal cascade welfare. Our mechanism selects an advertiser-position matching and a designated last ad, then randomly thins earlier ads so that each selected ad's expected cascade CTR is the same fraction of its standalone CTR. This yields an exact closed-form expression for expected welfare, which we maximize over a bid-independent lottery range using linear programming. Exact optimization ensures monotonicity, while a random-prefix decomposition proves the factor-two guarantee, which is tight for this range. We also show that exactly optimizing the previous welfare surrogate can violate monotonicity, and evaluate welfare and running time on synthetic instances.

title: Pooling interval-monitored step-stress accelerated life tests for reliability prediction: A failure-rate-based meta-analysis for the proportional hazards family
abstract: Reliability qualification often relies on several step-stress accelerated life tests conducted in separate campaigns, laboratories, or test rigs, each with its own stress profile, sample size, and inspection schedule, and with units inspected only periodically so that only failure counts between inspections are recorded. Existing meta-analysis methods combine several step-stress experiments but require exactly observed failure times. Methods for interval-inspected step-stress data, on the other hand, have been developed only for a single experiment. This paper develops a failure-rate-based meta-analysis framework for multiple interval-inspected step-stress experiments within the proportional hazards family, linking the experiments through a common underlying lifetime model and a log-linear stress-life relationship. Maximum likelihood estimators and confidence intervals are derived for the model parameters and for engineering quantities of interest at normal operating conditions, including mission reliability, mean time to failure, and lifetime quantiles such as the 0.10 quantile (B10 life). For the LED data, pooling the two tests reduced the RMSE of the estimated reliability at 5 hours by about 20% and that of the 0.10 quantile by about 66%, compared with the better single test. A misspecification study shows that the median is robust to the choice of lifetime distribution (relative bias below 6%), whereas tail quantiles can have a relative bias of up to 34% that does not vanish as the sample size increases, which is critical for warranty decisions. The methodology is illustrated with simulated data and with two step-stress tests of light-emitting diodes.

title: Conformal Prediction with Stable Measurement Mechanisms
abstract: In applications such as air-quality monitoring, inexpensive sensor readings can help predict pollutant concentrations measured by a separate reference instrument. We study how to adapt conformal prediction intervals to a new population when reference outcomes are available in the source data, but only sensor readings and context, such as weather conditions, are available in the target. We assume that the measurement distribution at a given outcome and context remains stable, while context frequencies and outcome distributions may change. This model is a particular form of causal mechanism shift. Its statistical restriction has been studied as sparse joint shift. Using established marginal matching, predictive adjustment, and weighted conformal calibration, we examine what this restriction contributes to coverage and interval length for continuous outcomes. Gaussian analyses show how measurement stability can identify outcome changes and how retaining context can shorten prediction intervals. For Gaussian models with known source mechanisms, we derive exact coverage formulas in the large-calibration limit while keeping the unlabeled target sample finite. These formulas explain when sharing a correction across contexts is preferable to fitting separate corrections, and why estimating outcome variability is particularly sensitive to weakly informative measurements. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian data show a coverage gain over covariate weighting at the same mean length and a length reduction of about $8\%$ relative to pooled label adjustment at comparable coverage. On the Air Quality dataset, controlled shifts yield coverage gains with longer intervals, while spring-to-autumn and year-over-year transfers show substantial undercoverage.

title: Testing for Essential Heterogeneity in the Marginal Treatment Effects Model
abstract: We propose a test for essential heterogeneity in the marginal treatment effects model without imposing additive separability. On the observed support of the propensity score, no essential heterogeneity implies that the conditional mean of the outcome is affine in the propensity score, and this affine restriction is the sharp testable implication of the null. We implement the test using a projected Gaussian-process statistic that is Neyman-orthogonal to the first-step estimation error, so the multiplier bootstrap avoids re-estimating nuisance parameters. Monte Carlo experiments show accurate size control and good power, and, unlike the fixed-scale integrated conditional moment benchmark, the data-driven median rule retains power as the conditioning set grows in dimension. In an application to the Ugandan ELA programme, the omnibus statistic rejects the null of no essential heterogeneity for aspirations at the midline follow-up.

title: Population-average trajectories and slopes in smooth random changepoint mixed models
abstract: Two-slope mixed-effects models with subject-specific changepoints are widely used to describe biphasic longitudinal trajectories. Treatment-arm summaries are often reported using a single "typical subject" curve obtained by plugging mean parameter values into the subject-specific model. This can be misleading when changepoint timing varies across individuals, because averaging subject-specific curves is not the same as evaluating one curve at average parameter values. A related issue is that individual trajectories may bend gradually rather than change slope through a literal kink, with transition sharpness varying between subjects. We propose population-average estimands for two-slope mixed models with random changepoints and smooth subject-level transitions. These estimands target the treatment-arm mean trajectory and instantaneous slope by averaging over fitted heterogeneity in changepoint timing and transition sharpness. We use a baseline-anchored normal-convolution soft hinge, which preserves the broken stick interpretation, includes the abrupt changepoint model as a limiting case, and allows analytic evaluation of the changepoint-marginalized kernels under a truncated normal changepoint distribution for fixed transition sharpness. Averaging over the fitted transition sharpness distribution is then performed by deterministic one-dimensional quadrature. In an application to HIV-1 RNA data from ACTG Protocol 315, with censoring and heavy-tailed residuals, the marginal summaries reveal a more gradual population-level transition than conventional plug-in summaries. The marginal slope remains more negative for longer, and the marginal mean continues to decline after the plug-in curve has begun to flatten. These results illustrate the main reporting implication: in random changepoint models, representative subject curves should not be treated as population-average trajectories or slopes.

title: Uncovering Latent Patterns in Program-Associated Library Attendance through Background Adjustment
abstract: Routinely collected library entrance records offer an opportunity to understand attendance patterns associated with library programs, but ordinary daily variation and detailed administrative user status categories complicate their interpretation. Building on a project-based learning collaboration with Kyushu University Central Library, we analyzed entrance records from October 2018 to July 2026. Descriptive analysis revealed relatively modest differences in attendance across the main weather categories, higher attendance on days with mean temperatures of 30{\deg}C or above, and pronounced differences between weekdays and weekends. To account for such background variation, we estimated expected attendance for each user status category and applied nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) to identify common patterns in positive background-adjusted responses from 92 events across 39 user status categories. Three interpretable response modes were identified: two concentrated on temporary external visitors and undergraduates, respectively, and one representing a broader combination of graduate student and research-related categories. The three-mode solution was selected by jointly considering held-out reconstruction error and basis stability across year-excluded fits. The identified modes also remained stable after excluding events from the selected COVID-19 period. The modes appeared in different combinations across individual events, with their dominance varying by program category. These findings illustrate how existing library records can reveal interpretable patterns of program-associated attendance without predefined grouping of user status categories.

title: Smart charging without rebound peaks: Wholesale price feedback limits distribution grid peaks from price-responsive electric vehicles
abstract: Studies on price-optimized EV charging consistently find that the common price signal synchronizes charging of the entire fleet of cars in the cheapest hours and creates new "rebound" load peaks in low-voltage grids. Almost all of these studies treat wholesale prices as exogenous, i.e., unaffected by the shifting EV load. This paper argues that this assumption overstates the problem: charging in low-price hours raises the wholesale price in those hours, which spreads charging across hours in equilibrium. I simulate price-optimized charging under real-time prices calibrated to German 2025 data. Even when adjusting for the increase in electricity demand, the coincident import peak of the local grid rises by 260%. After adding a model of equilibrium wholesale prices that takes the price-quantity feedback into account, the increase is reduced to a mere 5%. Allowing for vehicle-to-grid, the export peak rises by 115% under exogenous prices and falls by 6% under endogenous prices. The result holds across vehicle and charging parameters, charging constraints, renewable scenarios, network charges, price functions, peak measures, and simulation assumptions. Rebound peaks remain possible where vehicle adoption runs ahead of the national average or where charging power is high, but they are much smaller than the literature consensus suggests.

title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Functional Data: Wasserstein Risk Bounds and Diffusion-Based Conditional Generation
abstract: Functional data are costly to collect; samples of tens to hundreds of curves are common. Synthetic data augmentation can help, but its theory is developed for finite-dimensional data and relies on total variation, which is uninformative for functions. We study augmentation with a class-conditional functional diffusion generator and state guarantees in the Wasserstein-1 distance. For stable downstream estimators, we bound the risk of training on synthetic curves, from above and below, by the risk of training on as many real curves plus a generation penalty, and derive the best number of synthetic curves and a condition under which synthetic data outperform real data. For allocating synthetic curves under class imbalance, we bound the excess risk of training on real and synthetic curves together, without sample splitting. In applications to temperature, hyperspectral and gait curves, augmentation improved classification, function-to-scalar regression and function-to-function regression, and directing synthetic curves to the minority class gave the largest gain under class imbalance.

title: Distributional Counterfactual Dependence in the Special Sciences
abstract: Special-science explanations often concern distributions rather than individual outcomes. Since higher-level states depend on lower-level processes, what would make a higher-level explanation redundant? I argue that redundancy requires replacement without loss, not merely a reconstruction of individual outcomes. Distributional counterfactual dependence (DCD) identifies how changes in higher-level conditions alter an outcome distribution or a relevant feature of it. Against the background of stochastic supervenience, I distinguish this explanatory role from the dependence of higher-level states on lower-level bases. A replacement must be specified independently of the distribution to be explained and preserve the same counterfactual pattern at the grain and across the conditions relevant to the question. Applications to wage distributions, cognitive load, and selection clarify this requirement. A hypothetical comparison shows how a lower-level model can preserve the explanation and why matching selected outcome statistics may not suffice. DCD thus describes one form of non-reductive explanation that depends on counterfactual organization rather than additional higher-level productive powers.

title: The golden cage of science: first-last author prestige gap buys impact over disruption
abstract: First and last authors make critical but distinct contributions in the majority of scientific papers. First authors tend to conduct research and analysis, whereas last authors are usually responsible for setting research directions and providing resources and supervision. The first-last author prestige gap (FL gap, $\Delta H$) is defined as the H-index difference between the last and first authors prior to the focal paper's publication. The FL gap serves as a measure of the prestige asymmetry between the two dominant collaborators. We find that larger FL gaps in either direction are associated with higher impact and lower disruption. This trade-off is robust across team sizes and intensities of prior collaboration and can not be explained by first and last authors' separate prestige effects or their academic age gap. Further analysis shows that variation in last author prestige is associated with larger differences in both the article's impact and disruption than variation in first author prestige. We refer to this coexistence of higher impact and lower disruption related to the FL gap as the ``golden cage of science'', which reflects a common collaboration structure that statistically produces highly cited but less disruptive work. These findings suggest the first-last author prestige gap as an important indicator for examining how research teams balance senior guidance with exploratory autonomy.

title: Extreme proxies for causal identification: deconfounding with outliers
abstract: Causal identification under unobserved confounding typically relies on additional structure, such as a valid instrument or proxy variables. We show that heavy tailed variables offer an alternative route to identification by revealing treatment variation for which confounding becomes asymptotically negligible. Our key assumption is extreme propagation: when an unobserved confounder takes an extreme value, some observed variable in the system (called a safeguard) will become extreme with large probability. This way, selecting extreme treatment observations while safeguards remain non-extreme makes confounding asymptotically negligible relative to the treatment. We call this certification. We derive graphical conditions specifying which latent confounders must be monitored by safeguards and distributional conditions ensuring effective certification. The framework includes valid-instrument and double-proxy structures as special cases, as well as confounded instruments that are invalid in most approaches that do not exploit heavy tails. Geometrically, certification isolates the extremal ray whose slope equals the causal effect. This connects causal identification with multivariate extreme-value geometry and motivates a family of novel simple estimators. Simulations demonstrate performance gains under nonlinear confounding and heavy tails, while revealing limitations in light-tailed regimes (where cancellation can conceal extreme confounding from the safeguards). We validate our methodology in simulation studies and by recovering the ground-truth flow in a river discharge application.

title: Resolving the Mobility-Equity-Emissions Trilemma: A Causal Machine Learning Framework for Dynamic Tolling Policy
abstract: We propose a causal machine learning framework to integrate dynamic tolling for mobility, equity, and climate objectives, resolving a long-standing policy trilemma. Using Double Machine Learning, we estimate zone-type-specific treatment effects, showing that commercial zones yield nearly twice the delay reduction of residential zones. Our adaptive quota mechanism expands residential coverage 34-fold while preserving 93% of total delay savings and sustaining high return on investment. The framework delivers climate co-benefits, reducing emissions by 743.5 metric tons of CO2 (valued at 141 USD) via congestion-sensitive pricing under moderate traffic conditions with sensitivity bounds from 557.6 to 929.3 tons. Crucially, we uncover a policy-invariant toll range where performance remains robust across demand scenarios, simplifying implementation. This study reveals critical, previously unidentified insights, such as a policy-invariant toll range, that can significantly simplify real-world implementation. Validated on synthetic data mirroring real-world networks, our methodological advances lay the foundation for future public deployment.

title: On the Consistency of Spectral Clustering under Generalized Gaussian Mixture Models
abstract: Spectral clustering is a widely used clustering method with strong empirical performance and favorable computational scalability. Existing theory has established its consistency and risk guarantees under Gaussian and related mixture models, primarily in settings with relatively simple latent structure. In this paper, we study spectral clustering under a semiparametric Gaussian mixture model, where the observed data become Gaussian-mixture distributed only after unknown monotone coordinate-wise transformations. We derive non-asymptotic bounds for its cluster recovery error. As a byproduct of the theory, we show that spectral clustering provides a theoretically justified initialization for a broad class of high-dimensional mixture-based learning procedures.

title: Optimal Experimental Design for the Polynomial Maximization Method: a Higher-Order Reserve Beyond Second-Order Design Theory
abstract: Optimal designs for regression with asymmetric errors build on the second-order least squares estimator (SLSE) of Wang and Leblanc (2008), whose gain over ordinary least squares (OLS) comes from the error skewness. With i.i.d. errors the optimally weighted SLSE solves the same estimating equation as the degree-two Polynomial Maximization Method (PMM), a family whose degree-$S$ location estimator has asymptotic variance $g_S\le1$ times that of the sample mean. We derive optimal designs for this family when the errors are independent with constant variance but have standardised cumulants of order three and higher that vary with the regressor (cumulant heteroscedasticity). For a known reduction field $g_S(x)$, the $g_S$-weighted information matrix $M_{g_S}$ obeys the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem. A constant field leaves the OLS-optimal design unchanged; a non-constant field can change it but need not. For symmetric errors with varying kurtosis, the PMM$_2$ and conditional-SLSE designs cannot depart from the OLS-optimal one, whereas a degree-three design can. A stratify-and-pool PMM$_S$ estimator attains $N\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta)\to\sigma^2M_{g_S}^{-1}$ at every degree as all strata grow; its per-stratum reduction is below one only for symmetric errors with the symmetry imposed. For a quadratic model on $[0,1]$ with symmetric Beta errors of unit variance and dose-varying shape, the third-order design for the known field has $A$-efficiency $1.047$ relative to the OLS-optimal design, and $1.001$ under the $D$-criterion. A two-stage procedure that estimates the field from a one-third pilot builds designs of $A$-efficiency $1.014$-$1.020$ at $N=600$-$2400$; its realised mean-squared-error ratio against the OLS-optimal design ranges from $0.89$ (a loss) to $1.08$.

title: Near-boundary asymptotics for profile score statistics
abstract: We establish asymptotic results for profile score statistics under sequences of parameters that may tend to the boundary of the parameter set. When the likelihood is profiled over a set with boundary points, the distribution of the statistic can depend, even asymptotically, on a distance to the boundary that cannot be estimated consistently. We address this in three ways. First, we give conditions under which the nuisance score has a root on an extended parameter set, and the profile score statistic formed with that root converges to a chi-squared distribution. Second, we show that the efficient score statistic converges to a chi-squared distribution under a separate condition that can hold even for estimators constrained to the original set. Both lead to confidence regions with asymptotically correct coverage probability, uniformly on sets that may contain boundary points, and the conditions allow the scores for the interest and nuisance parameters to grow at different rates or become asymptotically collinear. Third, we quantify the coverage error of applying the profile score statistic without an extended set. We approximate the distribution of the statistic and bound the error by a quantity that decays like a normal tail in the standardized distance to the boundary. The approximation also gives one-sided tests with least favorable critical values whose asymptotic size is at most the nominal level. We illustrate the results in a zero-inflated Poisson model and a one-way random effects model.

title: The Computational Assessment Stack: An Architecture for AI-Native Measurement
abstract: Test development is shifting toward automation and agentic artificial intelligence (AI), in which autonomous systems draft items at scale, assemble test forms, administer adaptive assessments, score complex responses, and monitor test quality. As autonomous systems take on more of this work, the architecture underlying test development must change to preserve assessment quality under the new paradigm. This paper proposes the Computational Assessment Stack (CAS), a four-layer architecture for AI-native measurement where every stage of the assessment lifecycle shares a unifying computational construct representation as its base layer. This representation is a machine-readable, modular, and versioned knowledge graph. Three layers are built above it: computational content generation that builds on the knowledge graph; computational psychometrics that derives substantive structure directly from the knowledge graph; an orchestration layer in which agentic systems operationalize the stack under human governance. The paper's core contribution is architectural. Building on foundational psychometric frameworks, the CAS provides a persistent representation that unifies the four layers. Unlike the descriptive prose traditionally used to define constructs in test development, the proposed architecture renders measurement assumptions inspectable and their consequences empirically testable.

title: The Conditional Value of Costly Information in Collective-Risk Dilemmas
abstract: Many high-stakes collective problems, e.g., climate mitigation and pandemic response, share a structure in which risk materializes unless a group threshold is met. This threshold is often uncertain, but uncertainty can be reduced at a cost. We study this information cost tradeoff in an evolutionary game theoretic model of social learning in the collective-risk dilemma, where individuals must cooperate to reach a possibly uncertain threshold to prevent collective loss. Individuals may pay a fixed cost to observe the threshold's true value and condition their cooperation on it. Across four threshold priors, we characterize risk levels at which cooperative equilibria emerge and show that low cost information increases group success. However, this effect is reversed at higher costs. We define a private \emph{value of information} and show that information is worth buying only when it is considerably cheaper than contributing. When purchased information is shared with the group, the cooperative tipping point shifts to lower risk levels. Despite bearing a private cost, above this tipping point buyers earn more in expectation than information free-riders. We then study these dynamics when information diffuses through a network, allowing nodes to relay it. Although fewer individuals pay for information, relaying increases group success, and noisy relaying does not reduce it. By contrast, false information does, especially when it originates at the hubs of heterogeneous networks, and large attacks can bring collective action close to collapse. Buyers act as a firewall against disinformation, confining it to source neighbourhoods, and once disinformation sources are removed, the population recovers. The value of costly information thus depends on its price, the level of risk, and how it is shared, and, in our setting, the effort of acquiring it also protects the population against disinformation.

title: Resource competition and survival for random walkers on complex networks
abstract: We consider the problem of $W$ random walkers on a complex network where each walker requires an amount $\theta$ of resource at each time to survive. Resource is stochastically produced at each vertex of the network with a specified distribution. The survival time of the system of walkers is defined as the time required for all $W$ walkers to die. Using numerical simulations, we show that Erd{\H o}s-R\'enyi networks a have higher mean survival time than Scale-free networks as expected, but also that uniform distribution production leads to higher mean survival time than exponential distribution with the same mean. We derive an exact expression for the survival-time distribution under the assumption of independent walker lifespans, and use it to show that scale-free network topology produces strong dependence in the lifespans but homogeneous topology does not. We moreover demonstrate how the survival time can be substantially increased without changing the resource production or network topology by appropriately biasing the movement of the walkers towards low degree vertices on Scale-free networks, but has no effect on Erd{\H o}s-R{\'e}nyi networks.

title: AI-assisted design and analysis of experiments with unstructured treatments
abstract: Randomized experiments involving complex, unstructured treatments such as text, images, or video, are increasingly common in social science research. The goal of many of these studies is to estimate the effect of a structured, interpretable attribute that generalizes beyond the treatments used in the experiment (e.g., the presence of a linguistic or visual feature). There are two key challenges when conducting such studies: observed effects of the attribute of interest (i) may be confounded by other correlated attributes, leading to poor internal validity; and (ii) may not generalize beyond the treatments used in the experiment, leading to poor external validity. We propose a framework for designing experiments with unstructured treatments that leverages generative AI or large databases to sample treatments in a way that explicitly navigates the tradeoff between internal and external validity. We show how to conduct conservative asymptotic inference with a difference-in-means estimator, and develop a calibrated AI-assisted estimator that incorporates zero-shot AI predictions to improve precision without introducing bias. Throughout, we work in a finite population framework, where treatment assignment is the only source of randomness, and treat AI generations and predictions as black-boxes with no guarantees on their performance. We illustrate and evaluate our approach by designing two hypothetical experiments, one with text and another with images.

title: Geoeconomic Stress and European Defence Readiness
abstract: This study develops a country-level measure of the economic-industrial capacity of European NATO Allies to mobilise, replenish, maintain, and sustain military capability under strategic stress. The measure comprises four components: macroeconomic capacity, sectoral resilience, defence-industrial capability, and logistics and sustainment. The analysis covers 28 European Allies and evaluates a balanced baseline against five geoeconomic stress scenarios. The results distinguish baseline capacity from stress vulnerability and provide an assessment framework for identifying the economic-industrial bottlenecks that can constrain sustained military readiness. Baseline scores vary materially across countries, with a sample mean of 0.610 and a range from 0.471 to 0.759. The calibrated geoeconomic shocks reduce effective capacity in every scenario, though the effects are highly heterogeneous. The combined-stress scenario has the largest average effect, lowering the sample mean to 0.491, a decline of 19.5 per cent relative to baseline. TRS and PR operate mainly through defence-industrial and replenishment constraints; supply-chain fragmentation is driven primarily by sectoral exposure and substitutability; and external-support reduction operates through allied access and sustainment. Our results suggest shifting attention from expenditure targets alone towards the capacity to convert resources into usable military capability: the key issue is not only how much is spent, but also which bottlenecks limit the conversion of resources into capability.

title: Estimating Stability of Individual-Specific Predictions from AI-based prediction models using Bootstrap and Cross-validation Resampling
abstract: Clinical prediction models are typically developed in a single finite dataset, which is one of many possible datasets that could have been collected. Applying the same model development procedure in another sample will provide different predictions for an individual. The degree to which an individual's prediction varies across development sets is referred to as prediction instability and is not captured by average performance measures. Resampling of the training data offers a practical way to assess instability, but its ability to do so accurately and reliably for different model choices is unclear. In a simulation study, we considered non-parametric, parametric, and out-of-bag bootstrap methods and repeated 10-, 5-, and 2-fold cross-validation (CV) to estimate metrics of prediction instability for Elastic Net logistic regression and Random Forest. The same metrics estimated in independent development samples provided the reference. We assessed individual-level prediction variance, empirical 95% range width, and mean absolute differences from the original prediction and true outcome probability. Instability increased in smaller development samples, was greater for Random Forest, and varied across the probability range. Repeated 5- and 10-fold CV underestimated prediction instability across scenarios. Default non-parametric bootstrap more closely approximated independent sampling for Elastic Net but often overestimated instability for Random Forest, as did parametric bootstrap. Out-of-bag bootstrap and repeated 2-fold CV generally agreed most closely with independent sampling, although no procedure was uniformly best. Resampling procedures should not be used interchangeably, nor should less variable predictions be taken as evidence of greater stability. To estimate prediction instability, prefer procedures that predict on held-out data and limit overlap between training resamples.

title: Strategic Calibration in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Audited Pivot Scoring for Truthful Elicitation
abstract: In large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, reported confidence increasingly determines the allocation of scarce downstream attention, computation, and decision influence. This makes reporting strategic: an agent may overstate the relevance of its contribution even when its underlying belief is well calibrated. Existing calibration methods largely assume passive reporting and therefore do not address strategic incentives created when confidence determines downstream allocation. We formulate strategic calibration as a reporting-layer incentive problem and propose the Audited Pivot Scoring Mechanism (APSM). APSM offsets platform-controlled allocation benefits, uses inverse-propensity-weighted sparse audits, charges the Clarke pivot externality, and applies a strictly proper score. Under the stated model assumptions, truthful reporting is the unique expected-utility best response. We also characterize approximate execution and the audit-variance trade-off. Calculator-free experiments show that LLM agents inflate confidence under Top-$K$ incentives. With a shared agent-local utility interface, LLM agents reduce distortion under both Compensated Proper Scoring (CPS) and APSM. CPS achieves higher exact allocation match, whereas APSM yields lower Brier loss and numerically fewer cutoff crossings. Experiments further show that APSM enlarges the utility margin against allocation-changing deviations by $1.93\times$ and improves robustness under approximate execution. These results support incentive-aware elicitation as a distinct layer for reliable multi-agent coordination.

title: A Factor-6 Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanism for Cascade Position Auctions
abstract: Position auctions require assigning advertisers to positions and determining their display order. Under cascade behavior, earlier clicks prevent users from reaching later placements, coupling the click probabilities of selected advertisements. Existing methods achieve constant-factor welfare approximation and monotone logarithmic-factor approximation separately, leaving open whether both guarantees can be attained simultaneously. The difficulty is that welfare-preserving rounding need not maintain the monotonicity of individual click-through rates required for truthful bidding. We resolve this problem by developing a polynomial-time randomized mechanism that achieves a factor-6 welfare approximation and truthfulness in expectation for arbitrary public advertiser-position click probabilities. The mechanism optimizes a reach-weighted linear relaxation and converts its solution into feasible ordered allocations through matching decomposition, probability-bounded grouping, and calibrated attenuation. This construction compensates for cascade dependence and ensures that each advertiser's expected click-through rate equals exactly one sixth of its fractional click coordinate. The resulting identity transfers the monotonicity of the fractional allocation to the implemented mechanism, enabling exact incentive-compatible payments while preserving the welfare guarantee. The allocation lottery and payments are computable in polynomial bit time, with exact sampling in expected polynomial time.

title: An Integrated Framework for Assessing Interpretability in Exploratory Factor Analysis
abstract: Interpretability in Exploratory Factor Analysis is characterized by the fundamental trade-off between structural sparseness and explained common variance. Lacking formal evaluation metrics, researchers frequently sacrifice parsimony in the pattern matrix to maximize the model's explanatory coverage. For this reason, we extend Hoyer's sparseness ratio into a flexible \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal{L}_{p_1}/\mathcal{L}_{p_2}$}{Lp1/Lp2} formulation to introduce the Interpretability Index $I$, defined as the geometric mean of explained common variance and the generalized sparseness index. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of $I$ as norm orders increase, establishing that raising $p_2$ alone yields a stable limit, whereas increasing $p_1$ and $p_2$ jointly causes the measure to saturate. The canonical choice $(p_1,p_2)=(2,4)$ balances numerical stability with a smooth, tractable objective. We finally demonstrate, on five benchmark datasets from the statistical literature, how the Interpretability Index provides a systematic criterion for selecting the optimal parametrization of the latent space according to the user's analytical goals.

title: SoftBART-CORM Models for Density Regression
authors: Jim E. Griffin and Maria Kalli
abstract: Flexible modelling of the conditional distribution of a response given predictors is important in many applications where nonlinear effects, heteroskedasticity, and multimodality may be present. We introduce the SoftBART-CoRM, a predictor-dependent infinite mixture model that combines the interpretable component structure of Compound Random Measures (CoRMs) with SoftBART priors on both mixture weights and component-specific parameters. The model flexibly captures complex distributional features, while global--local shrinkage and predictor-selection priors mitigate overfitting and identify the covariates driving component allocation and kernel parameters. Posterior inference is performed using an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that leverages existing \texttt{R} implementations of SoftBART. Through simulation studies and real-data applications, we show that the proposed approach can adaptively shrink towards simpler mixture representations, provide interpretable inference on the predictors governing different aspects of the conditional distribution, and achieve superior out-of-sample predictive performance relative to benchmark models.

title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models
abstract: Prediction is one of the most important research topics in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, in the domain of streaming data analysis, real-time prediction has become a rapidly growing research field in recent years, owing to the abundance of streaming data. In many fields of scientific research, such as biomedical research, weather forecasting, and traffic management, improving real-time prediction of streaming data is crucial in general. However, the complicated features of streaming data, such as large-scale and high-velocity, impose both theoretical and computational challenges to the development and evaluation of real-time prediction in this field, especially when the investigator has multiple models at hand. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel Renewable Model Averaging method through Quadratic approximation (ReMAQ) for generalized linear model (GLM) for streaming data. By approximating the model averaging procedure for GLMs (which is typically a convex optimization problem) with a quadratic optimization formulation, ReMAQ allows us to update the model averaging prediction sequentially when a new batch of data arrives, without accessing the entire historical data. Moreover, ReMAQ is also computationally efficient as one only needs to consider a quadratic programming problem in each steps of updating. Under certain regular conditions, we also show that the proposed ReMAQ weight is asymptotically equivalent to that by the oracle model averaging based on the inaccessible full data, the asymptotic optimality of ReMAQ is then established accordingly. The proposed method is also assessed by simulation studies. We apply our proposed ReMAQ in the study of the Airline On-Time Performance Dataset and the results demonstrate the superiority our method in practical situations.

title: Multiplicity and Uniqueness of Equilibria in Continuous-Time Dynamic Discrete Games
authors: Jason R. Blevins and Youngjae Jeong
abstract: We consider multiplicity and uniqueness of equilibria in continuous-time dynamic discrete games where players move sequentially according to independent Poisson processes. With multiple equilibria, the structural model is incomplete: the reduced form and counterfactual predictions depend on how equilibria are selected. We provide closed-form sufficient conditions for uniqueness of Markov perfect equilibrium in this class of games. The conditions are semiparametric and can be verified from model primitives. To measure the coverage of the conditions and characterize multiplicity more broadly, we carry out a large-scale numerical search for equilibria of a dynamic duopoly model of entry and exit. Although uniqueness is the norm in our broad search, we find that multiplicity concentrates in economically relevant regions: where the market cannot profitably sustain both firms, where firms are very patient, and at intermediate decision frequencies that balance strategic interaction and commitment. When multiplicity is present, we typically find two stable asymmetric equilibria and one unstable symmetric equilibrium. Monte Carlo and counterfactual simulations show this structure matters for empirical work. A full-solution estimator that assumes uniqueness can converge to the unstable equilibrium, even when the data were generated by a stable one, while a two-step estimator recovers the correct equilibrium.

title: Jointly Modeling Preferences and Imperfect Decision-Making in Large Language Models
abstract: Do preferences Large Language Models (LLMs) express in standard elicitation tasks predict their strategic behaviour? LLM agents interacting with humans and other AI systems face potentially conflicting objectives, such as individual welfare, group welfare, and environmental concerns. Prior work characterizes LLM preferences through behavioral-economic and psychological elicitation or strategic games, but rarely tests consistency across settings and prediction in other strategic environments. This requires modeling how competing objectives jointly shape behavior, whereas existing approaches typically measure preference dimensions in isolation. Drawing on utility theory, we introduce the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM), which combines a preference representation with mechanisms capturing imperfect utility maximization. We formulate estimation as an inverse-game problem, jointly inferring preferences and behavioral parameters from observed choices. We evaluate PBM in three social dilemmas that expose conflicting motives: a Public Goods Game, a Collective-Risk Dilemma, and a Common-Pool Resource dilemma. We find that while preferences estimated from established behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict behavior in these dilemmas, models fitted in one dilemma retain predictive value in others, suggesting that inferred preferences capture meaningful aspects of LLM decision-making that elicitation instruments may miss. Finally, we assess alignment with persona instructions, finding that inferred preferences broadly reflect intended priorities with specific divergences across dimensions, LLMs, and games being identified by our approach. Our methodology provides a framework for studying how consistently LLM preferences explain behavior, assessing alignment with intended priorities, and revealing trade-offs and behavioral patterns that standard elicitation may miss.

title: Identification and curvature bias for shared inputs in multichannel dynamical models
abstract: Pooling many channels with a shared unknown input can leave persistent bias when each channel retains a fixed number of observations and its own incidental parameters. For heterogeneous smooth channel manifolds under isotropic noise, the second-order bias is an information-weighted regression of mean curvature on normal input velocity. A feasible correction gives centred Gaussian inference as the noise level $\sigma$ decreases with $R\sigma^6\to0$, compared with $R\sigma^2\to0$ without correction. We extend the stochastic expansion and studentization to deterministic channel arrays with densely correlated Gaussian errors of bounded covariance operator norm. General marginal covariance adds a forcing term that can bias even flat channels, while cross-channel covariance changes uncertainty. For Gaussian errors with a separable frame-by-channel covariance whose channel factor is autoregressive in a known ordering, an independent zero-mean calibration field yields a covariance estimator accurate enough for corrected inference. Boundary accumulation and fixed working population models introduce distinct bias terms; rational-multiplier and zero-count arguments connect identification to frame-integrated compartment models. Simulations test both oracle and estimated-covariance inference, including independent PET replications. Moderate-noise undercoverage, optimization ambiguity and the need to validate reconstruction covariance limit practical inference. The real-data example supports sensitivity analysis, not clinically calibrated intervals.

title: Allocation Before the Clock: Graph, Set and Game Theory of Professional League of Legends Objective Setups
abstract: Before every neutral objective in professional League of Legends, each team decides which of its five players walk to the pit, which hold a lane, and when to commit. The leading analysis of such setups, TAGNet for Counter-Strike 2, clusters graph-network embeddings of player positions and reads cluster win rates as tactical quality. We treat a setup as an allocation on a walled map: formations are set partitions on the lattice $\Pi_5$, control is a geodesic Voronoi split of a navigation graph, and commitment is an allocation game solved as a quantal response equilibrium priced in win probability. On all 164 games of MSI and Worlds 2025 (2,994 team-setups, minimap tracks validated against Riot positions), trailing teams leave the pit empty far more often than leading teams, by +34.8 percentage points at the first baron and +30.4 percentage points at Atakhan. Our model, HASSE-QRE, finds six setup patterns that whole-model series-bootstrap refits reproduce (ARI 0.819, comparable to 0.813 for TAGNet's $K$-Means step alone) and indicates that teams price fights, travel and committed players, not the objective itself (weight 0.018; fixing it to one costs 59.9 log-likelihood points). The equilibrium reproduces a quarter of the commitment gap, almost all of it through state variables rather than its strategic channels. Weighting a team-level contrast by exposure moves it across $p=0.05$ (0.046 against 0.052). We release the tracks, setups and code.

title: From Average Effects to Proportions Benefiting: A Tutorial on ETZ-Powered Counterfactual Individual Benefit Analysis
abstract: Consider the question: "Is it true that at least 80% of patients would benefit more from receiving a new treatment, $Rx$, than from receiving a standard treatment, $C$?" Conventional treatment efficacy analyses based on average treatment effects cannot directly answer this question. Yet, even if the true mean treatment effects were known exactly, the answer to this question could still be either "yes" or "no", depending on the variability in patients' treatment responses and the dependence between their potential outcomes. This tutorial introduces a proportion-based perspective on individualized treatment benefit through the ETZ-powered Counterfactual Individual Benefit Analysis framework. We present two metrics, the individual benefit probability and the individual benefit lower bound, which enable confidence-based assessments of whether a prespecified proportion of patients achieves a clinically meaningful treatment benefit. We develop these metrics in both the factual random-pair and counterfactual same-patient settings. In particular, the ETZ decomposition provides a transparent characterization of different sources of outcome variability and enables more precise uncertainty quantification for counterfactual treatment comparisons. We illustrate the framework and its practical implementation using patient-level data from a Phase II randomized clinical trial. By shifting the focus from average treatment effects to population proportions of individual benefit, this tutorial provides a complementary perspective for evaluating treatment efficacy and informing individualized treatment decisions while controlling the type I error rate at a prespecified level.

title: Conference Design for Consensus under KL Acceptance
abstract: We study consensus formation and information acquisition in conferences where DeGroot-type opinion updating is constrained by an acceptance rule based on Kullback-Leibler divergence. Players choose private information experiments before deliberation, and these choices determine both their posterior distributions and acceptance tolerances. We establish sufficient conditions for global consensus under specified conference structures, including repeated bilateral conferences organized by a fully receptive mediator. Under full reimbursement of the mediator's conference costs, the information-acquisition game has a weighted potential and admits a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. We develop a numerical procedure using verified payoff bounds over the continuous posterior domain to certify approximate equilibria and assess partial reimbursement policies that preserve a given equilibrium profile. The binary state, three-player examples illustrate how conference order interacts with state variance. At larger variances in the tested range, placing the demanding nonmediator last is associated with lower conference costs and lower certified sufficient planner reimbursement, but greater information acquisition expenditure by the mediator. These findings reveal a trade-off between the planner's fiscal expenditure and the mediator's private burden, and show that the conference structure matters economically.

title: Causal Inference in Metric Spaces via Distance Profiles
abstract: Modern interventions increasingly produce object-valued outcomes, such as distributions, covariance matrices, networks, and trees. Existing causal frameworks often exploit special geometry such as one-dimensional Wasserstein quantiles or geodesic Fr\'echet means, whereas metric statistics studies random objects without confounding adjustment. We propose the profile causal effect $\Delta(\omega,t)$, which describes where and at what scale a treatment shifts probability mass, including changes in dispersion, tails, or structure that leave mean-level summaries unchanged. Formally, $\Delta(\omega,t)=\Pr\{d(\omega,Y(1))\le t\}-\Pr\{d(\omega,Y(0))\le t\}$ contrasts the potential-outcome probabilities of the same anchor-centered metric ball and requires no structure beyond the metric. On grids fixed by a deterministic or auxiliary design, we combine cross-fitted doubly robust scores with high-dimensional Gaussian approximation and the multiplier bootstrap to obtain simultaneous confidence bands and a global test under regularity conditions. The bands bound treatment-induced changes in ball and shell probabilities simultaneously and, at fixed anchors, extend to all radii. A protocol guides the choice of anchors and radii. Across the experiments, the global test detects concentration effects that mean-quantile and Fr\'echet-mean summaries miss. Its empirical size is near or below the nominal level, even under confounding, where naive metric tests are substantially oversized.

title: Approximate Quantile Factor Models
abstract: Weakly dependent idiosyncratic errors are standard in mean factor models, but quantile factor models have been analyzed only under independence. The mean-case definition of weak dependence, a bound on the eigenvalues of the error covariance matrix, does not carry over: I show that it neither implies nor is implied by the property that controls quantile estimation, since uncorrelated errors can share a pervasive quantile component. I instead define approximate quantile factor models through a concentration condition on the idiosyncratic array. Under it, the quantile factor analysis (QFA) estimator is consistent at a rate that deteriorates by the square root of a dependence constant, which is minimax optimal, and the number of factors is consistently estimated. Dependence changes the asymptotic variance, for which I provide HAC and thresholded estimators. Monte Carlo experiments confirm these predictions. In FRED-QD and FRED-MD, standard errors ignoring dependence understate uncertainty, most strongly in the tails.

title: More Meters or More Prices? One- vs. Multi-dimensional Fee Mechanisms on Ethereum
abstract: Permissionless blockchains use transaction fee mechanisms to allocate the resources that transactions consume, such as execution, data bandwidth, and state creation. Recent blockchain designs explore pricing these resources separately rather than through a single unit. We study this shift on Ethereum, whose roadmap moves in stages from a one-dimensional fee mechanism to a multi-dimensional one. We build a demand model for the three resources, calibrated from Ethereum's 2025 block-capacity increases, and find that state creation is the most price-responsive. We then evaluate both mechanisms at higher block capacity, combining the model with transaction-level metering reconstruction and block-level simulation. Under a one-dimensional mechanism, state creation determines the fee and suppresses execution throughput. Adjusting how state is metered can align resource usage under constant demand, but a single fee cannot track all resources when demand varies, leaving all underutilized. A multi-dimensional mechanism removes this fee coupling, but execution still generates data that must be propagated. Across different allocations between block execution and propagation time, the multi-dimensional mechanism delivers 4--34\% more execution throughput at similarly low congestion, with higher target utilization and state growth near its intended level.

title: Efficiency vs Capability in the Intelligence Explosion
abstract: AI progress can feed back into AI research in two ways. Capability improvements allow AIs to perform a larger share of AI research tasks, while efficiency improvements raise AI research output per unit of compute on tasks already automated. In a task automation model of AI research, I show that a software-driven intelligence explosion - a self-sustaining acceleration in AI progress with fixed compute and human labor - requires both margins to improve sufficiently fast, and neither margin can substitute for the other. To see whether these conditions hold, I calibrate both margins with data on recent AI progress. I estimate that capability progress is likely fast enough to support an SIE, while efficiency progress is on the knife-edge. In Monte Carlo simulations, an SIE occurs in 49% of draws, indicating that an SIE is plausible but uncertain based on historical trends in AI progress. The single largest source of uncertainty is the rate of efficiency progress, whose uncertainty is responsible for 45% of the uncertainty about whether an SIE occurs, more than all other parameters combined. Thus, better data on efficiency progress in frontier models is essential for understanding the likelihood of an SIE.

title: Compiling and forecasting implied volatility surfaces via survey sampling, tempered inverse-probability sequence learning, and causal activity clocks
abstract: Compiling implied volatility (IV) surfaces and forecasting derivative risk from high-frequency equity and options feeds requires addressing contract heterogeneity, schema shifts, volatility clustering, and non-stationary trading activity. Using a split-adjusted NVIDIA (NVDA) equity and options panel (2018-2025), this study integrates finite-population survey sampling, tempered inverse-probability sequence learning, and causal activity clocks. Four findings emerge. First, cross-sectional surface accuracy depends on matching the sampling design to the target functional: plug-in stratified allocations using lagged cell dispersion improve equal-weighted surface reconstruction with full grid coverage, whereas liquidity-weighted probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling excels on liquidity-weighted targets by construction yet inflates error when misapplied. Second, in longitudinal LSTM sequence training, PPS and Neyman designs retain more tail-volatility windows than simple random sampling (SRS); all three designs are equivalent to full-census training within chosen margins while cutting training time, though incremental forecasting gains of informative selection over SRS are not established. Third, out-of-sample evaluation shows a predictability contrast: short-horizon prices are not forecastable beyond a random walk with drift among tested models, whereas forward IV shows descriptive mean-reversion skill concentrated in a few post-shock reversal sessions (insignificant under session-clustered tests), with sequence models not beating a linear HAR-IV benchmark and feature pruning driving stability. Fourth, across a 6.3x start-to-end (nearly twentyfold trough-to-peak) price expansion, rolling volume and dollar clocks stabilize bar rates and compress intraday return kurtosis beyond diurnal scaling.

title: Nonparametric shrinkage estimation of high-dimensional variance component matrices
abstract: We develop a nonparametric spectral estimation method for variance component covariance matrices in high-dimensional multivariate mixed effects models. Although classical MANOVA estimators are unbiased entrywise, their eigenvalues can be severely dispersed and biased when the number of traits is comparable to the number of realizations of the random effects. Building on a system of self-consistent equations that characterizes the limiting spectral distribution of a MANOVA estimator, we construct a kernel-based nonlinear transformation of the sample eigenvalues that targets the optimal rotation-invariant estimator under Frobenius loss. The resulting procedure corrects for high-dimensional eigenvalue spreading without imposing a parametric model on the unknown covariance spectrum. Our work is motivated by applications in quantitative genetics, where estimating genetic covariance components across many phenotypic traits is of central interest. We implement the method in a new Python package mlmm-shrinkage and compare the proposed estimator with classical estimators across several common experimental designs in this domain through simulations and a real-data application.

title: Faithful Federated Tabular Data Synthesis
abstract: Synthetic data is an important data source in the AI era. This paper studies the generation of mixed-type tabular synthetic data in federated settings, where two key challenges arise: ensuring distributional fidelity and effectively handling mixed-type data. We propose Federated Integrative Two-Step Synthesis (FITS), a framework for mixed-type tabular data synthesis. At its core is a two-step federated algorithm for estimating conditional cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) using local linear regression. Building on this algorithm, we develop a federated synthesis procedure based on the probability chain rule to ensure distributional fidelity. To handle mixed-type data, FITS introduces a continualization method that lifts discrete variables into a continuous space and recovers their discrete distributions without loss at both the density-function and CDF levels. This transformation provides a unified continuous representation of mixed-type variables, facilitating the application of local linear regression and synthetic data generation. Our theoretical analysis characterizes the conditional density and cumulative distribution functions of the continualized mixed-type variables and establishes the uniform convergence of the resulting federated conditional CDF estimators. Experiments demonstrate that FITS-generated synthetic data improves downstream task performance for all clients, with the benefits depending on how the synthetic data is used.

title: Exhaustive adjustment-set selection and causal effects for distribution-valued outcomes, with inference under latent Gaussian spatio-temporal dependence
abstract: Selecting adjustment covariates for a distribution-valued outcome must preserve dependence that scalar summaries can discard, and surveillance outcomes are also dependent across space and time. Under unconfoundedness and a relative-overlap condition we identify average treatment effects, stochastic and incremental intervention effects, and natural direct and indirect effects for such outcomes, with doubly and triply robust scores. For independent data, adjustment sets are selected exhaustively by distance-covariance sufficient dimension reduction: we give a root-n projector expansion, a basis-invariant criterion tensor, and a simultaneous outer confidence collection calibrated by fractional sampling with a finite-population correction. For dependence, units are functions of a latent Gaussian field, exponential in space and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck in time, plus independent noise. Such data are $\rho$-mixing at an exponential rate, and the covariance between any two square-integrable scores is a power series in the latent correlation with positive semidefinite coefficients. Consequences include a central limit theorem for all the causal estimators, the exact undercoverage of independence-based intervals, a consistent Mehler covariance estimator under finite chaos order, and an asymptotically conservative convex-chord estimator; block fractional sampling extends the collection under an assumed linearization. In simulations, fractional sampling raises weak-signal collection coverage from .69-.78 to at least .98 while retaining nearly all candidate sets, and the dependence-aware estimators substantially reduce undercoverage, although none is exact when few units fall within a correlation range. A descriptive analysis of U.S. syphilis surveillance and Medicaid expansion illustrates the estimands and compares dependence-aware with conventional inference.

title: Fitting time-varying parameter models via partially noncentered parametrizations
abstract: Time-varying parameter (TVP) models are widely used to capture evolving relationships but inference is often computationally demanding due to high-dimensional latent states. The efficiency of iterative algorithms depends critically on the choice of latent state augmentation, with centering preferred for genuinely time-varying coefficients and noncentering favored when coefficients are nearly constant. We propose a partially noncentered parametrization that bridges these extremes via dimension-specific working parameters for both location and scale. Optimal working parameters are derived by analyzing EM convergence rates, and an alternating expectation-conditional maximization algorithm is developed to implement the approach. As the convergence rate of mean-field variational Bayes (MFVB) is closely related to EM, we extend the approach to develop partially noncentered MFVB algorithms for the TVP model, placing triple gamma priors on baseline coefficients and process variances to induce shrinkage. Simulations and empirical applications show that the resulting MFVB algorithms yield posterior approximations closer to Markov chain Monte Carlo than conventional centered or noncentered parametrizations. We also develop an efficient solver for the block tridiagonal inverse matrices arising in the proposed algorithms.

title: Observable Self-Restraint in Repeated Cheap Talk
abstract: A long-lived sender repeatedly advises a myopic receiver who observes only the recommendation record. Nonbinding, observable self-restraint, such as a rolling quota on favorable recommendations, makes each favorable recommendation use capacity that could serve future opportunities, inducing selective advice. With two actions, when obedience requires a strictly positive cost of self-restraint, the sender's normalized equilibrium payoff is subject to a ceiling equal to the payoff from the best credible partitional signal minus the expected cost of self-restraint. This bound holds at every discount factor; under an upper-tail condition, rolling quotas approach it as the sender becomes patient. A sufficiently valuable opportunity can also induce an informative violation that ends communication.

title: Recursive moment updates for scalable Bayesian nonparametric regression
abstract: Bayesian nonparametric regression methods have wide applications in statistics and machine learning, but inference can often be expensive or require approximations. This paper introduces a class of recursive moment function updates which are closed form, interpretable, expedient, and fully quantify Bayesian uncertainty through the martingale posterior. The proposed recursive updates can be used off-the-shelf and encompass challenging scenarios such as nonparametric heteroscedasticity, heavy-tailed or skewed noise, and importantly generalize to the multi-output case with missing outcomes without any significant loss in tractability or speed. We show frequentist consistency under weak assumptions in the aforementioned scenarios, and demonstrate empirically that our proposed method is orders of magnitude faster than competing Bayesian nonparametric approaches, with competitive or even superior prediction and estimation accuracy.

title: Joint Service Depth and Priority Design in Queueing Systems
abstract: In AI-assisted service systems, the server can choose how much processing effort to spend on each job, which we call the service depth. Deeper reasoning improves output quality but occupies the server longer and increases congestion, and the realized processing time remains random because AI models are probabilistic and tasks vary in complexity. We study the joint design of service depth and priority in a single-server queue whose customers differ in delay sensitivity, with the goal of maximizing social welfare. For each customer type, the decision maker chooses a priority level and a service depth, and service times are exponential with mean equal to the chosen depth. With two customer types and linear service values, we characterize the centralized optimum. Counterintuitively, it prioritizes the patient type and gives it a smaller service depth when patient customers are sufficiently prevalent. When delay sensitivity is private, however, incentive compatibility requires the impatient type to receive a weakly shorter sojourn time, so the optimal price menu never prioritizes the patient type. Consequently, there can be a welfare gap between the centralized decision maker's optimal control policy and the optimal decentralized pricing mechanism. With a continuum of types, the centralized optimum is monotone: more delay-sensitive customers receive weakly smaller depth and higher priority, so the optimum can be implemented by a price menu with no welfare loss. Allowing randomized depths similarly closes the gap in the two-type model. Finally, we calibrate an agentic AI service system using published coding-agent trials from DeepSWE and numerically examine priority inversion, the value of joint design, and the welfare gain from personalization.

title: TempShap: When and How Much a Feature Matters in Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Attribution for a time-series forecaster should answer two questions that a feature-level scalar cannot: when in the input window a feature acts, and how much its influence changes across the forecast horizon. Most existing Shapley explainers treat each feature as one player and therefore collapse both axes. We propose TempShap, a retrospective, loss-based Shapley framework whose players are the individual input cells $(t,i)$. Its attribution tensor yields temporal-localization and horizon-impact profiles. We validate these against planted temporal structures, a tractable exact cell game, and a closed-form attribution oracle for a real linear forecaster. Permutation sharing estimates the cell-level game at localized perturbation cost. Under redundant inputs, one-at-a-time scores under-credit substitutable information, whereas the signed Shapley decomposition preserves total value and yields more reliable held-out deletion rankings under mean masking. A planted counterexample isolates the redundancy mechanism. Experiments show a deletion-ranking advantage across Shapley estimators, forecasting benchmarks, and model families.
